data.body:
AC5 confirmed by a live outage, unplanned — the alarm design proved itself under real conditions
within the hour.

Timeline, all measured:

    2026-09-04 17:42 PDT   bridge_run_failures = 1.0    (Reconcile Bridge run failed, 01:33 UTC)
    2026-09-04 18:42 PDT   bridge_run_failures = 1.0    (second consecutive failure, 02:34 UTC)
    2026-09-04 ~18:5x PDT  rebar-bridge-run-failures    OK -> ALARM

Before this, six consecutive healthy runs published an explicit `0.0` (11:23 through 16:23 PDT).

So the full contract executed end to end on live data: a healthy pass publishes 0 and breaks the
streak; a single failure does NOT alarm (deliberately — usually a transient API blip); the SECOND
consecutive failure transitions to ALARM. That is exactly the behaviour documented at
`monitoring_bridge.tf:53-64`, and it is why `notBreaching` is safe on this particular alarm: with
an explicit zero published on every healthy run, missing data is distinguishable from healthy
rather than being conflated with it.

**Recording a correction to my own earlier reading.** When I first saw this alarm sitting at OK
during the outage I read it as this ticket's dead-man inversion caught in the act, and I was
wrong twice over — the alarm needs two consecutive failures, and the metric is published on both
paths. I only avoided filing that false finding by querying the datapoints instead of reasoning
from the alarm state. The distinction matters for this ticket specifically: "alarm is OK during a
known-bad condition" is the SYMPTOM of a dead-man inversion, but it is equally the symptom of an
alarm that is correctly waiting for its evaluation criteria. Only the published series tells them
apart.

The outage itself is tracked separately as `bairnish-sunbeamed-nandine` (`5c5c-5741-9b33-47fa`) —
the ACLI 1200-issue ceiling. This comment concerns only the monitoring behaviour, which worked.
